items.title: Measuring the Mean Absolute Deviation of a Data Set From a Dot Plot

sections.normalized_html: The dot plot below shows the total time members of a rock band practiced their instruments last week. Each dot represents a different band member. What is the mean absolute deviation in the band members' practice times?
sections.readable_text:
The dot plot below shows the total time members of a rock band practiced their instruments last week. Each dot represents a different band member. What is the mean absolute deviation in the band members' practice times?

[IMG: /graphics/a045b479d291f2d09d15050c9ceabd29]

sections.normalized_html:
The dot plot tells us the following:

  • [MATH: 1] member practiced for [MATH: 3] hours

  • [MATH: 1] member practiced for [MATH: 4] hours

  • [MATH: 1] member practiced for [MATH: 5] hours

  • [MATH: 2] members practiced for [MATH: 6] hours

  • [MATH: 1] member practiced for [MATH: 9] hours

So, we get the following data:

[MATH: 3, \: 4, \: 5, \: 6, \: 6, \: 9]

Now, we find the mean of the data: [MATH: mean|= ((3 × 1) + (4 × 1) + (5 × 1) + (6 × 2) + (9 × 1))/(6); = (33)/(6); = 5.5]

Next, we subtract the mean from each number in the data set, find the absolute value of the results, and add all these together:

[MATH: |3 − 5.5|+|4 − 5.5|+|5 − 5.5|+|6 − 5.5|+|6 − 5.5|+|9 − 5.5||=;|− 2.5|+|− 1.5|+|− 0.5|+|0.5|+|0.5|+|3.5||=; 2.5 + 1.5 + 0.5 + 0.5 + 0.5 + 3.5|=; 9]

Finally, to calculate the mean absolute deviation (MAD), we divide the sum obtained above ([MATH: {\color{red}9}]) by the total number of data points ([MATH: 6]). This gives [MATH: \text{MAD} = \dfrac{\color{red}9}{6} = 1.5.]
